# Decoupling Resource Consumption from Economic Growth: A Comparative Study of China, Europe, and the United States

## Abstract

This article presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the relationship between economic growth and resource consumption, with a focus on the degree of decoupling in three major global economies: China, Europe, and the United States. As the global community faces pressing sustainability and environmental challenges, understanding how economic development intersects with resource utilisation in these regions has become increasingly critical. Previous research on decoupling has largely assumed positive economic growth; however, some countries have experienced periods of negative growth over the last two decades. This study extends decoupling criteria to incorporate such scenarios. The analysis begins with an examination of the interplay between economic growth, population growth, and domestic material consumption, followed by a detailed decoupling assessment. Results indicate that while China has made significant strides in improving resource efficiency over the past decade, its performance still lags behind that of the United States and Europe due to its stage of development. Nevertheless, China has demonstrated the most significant improvement in decoupling economic growth from material consumption, particularly during the second decade of the study period. Over the past 20 years, China has made notable advances in decoupling fossil fuel and metallic minerals consumption. By contrast, the United States (while showing the highest overall level of decoupling) has experienced a decline in performance, especially with respect to metallic and non-metallic minerals. Europe, meanwhile, has maintained a relatively stable decoupling trend.

## INTRODUCTION

Over the past 50 years, global material consumption (including fossil fuels, minerals, non-metallic minerals, and biomass) has more than tripled (UNEP-IRP, 2024 , 2019) . If current resource utilisation practices persist without significant and immediate reform, material extraction is projected to increase by nearly 60% by 2060, rising from 100 billion tons in 2020 to 160 billion tons (UNEP-IRP, 2024). This growth far exceeds the levels required to meet basic human needs as envisioned in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (Ma et al., 2025; United Nations, 2023 , 2015) .

The extraction and processing of materials are major drivers of environmental degradation, contributing to over half of global greenhouse gas emissions and a substantial share of particulate matter-related health impacts (Hertwich, 2021; Y. Wang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2019) . When accounting for land-use changes, these impacts intensify, with biomass being the largest contributor, followed by fossil fuels, non-metallic minerals, and metals (Tzachor et al., 2024; H. Wang et al., 2024) . Biomass, particularly from agriculture and forestry, is also the primary cause of biodiversity loss and water stress associated with land use (Pereira et al., 2024) . Moreover, international trade has exacerbated these crises (Lenzen et al., 2012; Wiedmann and Lenzen, 2018) . Overall, the environmental impacts linked to resource use continue to escalate.

In response to this challenge, the United Nations emphasises the decoupling of resource utilisation from economic growth as a central objective of its SDGs (UNEP, 2014; United Nations, 2015) . SDGs 8 and 12 specifically call for sustainable production and consumption practices to ensure resource sustainability, with SDG 12 also emphasising sustainability within supply chains. In parallel, SDG 7 advocates the transition to affordable and clean energy.

At the national and regional levels, China, Europe, and the United States, as the world's largest economies, dominate global resource consumption (Krausmann et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2024; Schandl et al., 2018; Wiedmann et al., 2015) and waste emissions (Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; W. Wang et al., 2024; Z. Wang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025) . Despite their collective dominance, these economies differ significantly in their economic structures and development trajectories. A targeted decoupling analysis is essential to identify pathways for achieving sustainable resource use under their distinct development models.

Existing decoupling analysis methods primarily focus on the relationship between economic growth and environmental impacts under varying national conditions. In recent years, the importance of decoupling analysis has grown significantly (Li et al., 2024) , with research efforts spanning multiple domains, including resource consumption (Jia et al., 2021; Song et al., 2020; H. Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2016) , energy consumption (Chen et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2015) , water consumption (Tian et al., 2016) , carbon emissions (Chen et al., 2018; Jalles, 2022; Jiang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019 Wang et al., , 2018;; Xu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020) , and integrated environmental impacts (Liang et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2019) . However, these studies predominantly examine the decoupling of environmental impacts from economic growth, often overlooking the impact of economic recessions. To address this gap, an enhanced decoupling analysis model was developed, capable of assessing decoupling under diverse economic conditions, extending beyond growth -centric frameworks.

This study applies the improved decoupling analysis model to evaluate resource consumption and economic growth across China, the United States, and Europe from 2000 to 2019. The analysis focuses on four key resource categories: fossil fuels, metallic minerals, non-metallic minerals, and biomass. The findings contribute to the global discourse on sustainable resource management and establish a foundation for adapting this model to various environmental and economic scenarios.

### Decoupling Analysis Method

In addition to presenting descriptive statistics for population, gross domestic product (GDP), and domestic material consumption (DMC) across these three major economic regions, this study aimed to quantify the degree of decoupling between economic activity and material consumption. Domestic Material Consumption (DMC) is an indicator used to measure the total amount of materials directly used by an economy. It represents all the raw materials extracted within a country's territory (which includes biomass, metals, minerals, and fossil fuels), plus what it imports from abroad, minus what it exports to other countries.

By decoupling economic activity from material consumption, it is understood as the process by which an economy is able to grow (measured typically through indicators such as GDP) while stabilising or reducing the amount of material resources it consumes. In a decoupled economic system, value can be created with lower inputs of raw materials.

According to Wang et al., 2013, the relationship between economic activity and resource consumption can be categorised into three scenarios, assuming positive GDP growth (g > 0) during the analysed period t 0 to t 1 : a) If the DMC decreases and the rate of DMC per unit of GDP (DMC/GDP) also decreases, then it is said that there is absolute decoupling.

b) If the DMC increases but the rate of DMC per unit of GDP (DMC/GDP) decreases, then it is said that there is relative decoupling. c) If the DMC grows and the rate of DMC per unit of GDP (DMC/GDP) also grows, then it is said that there is no decoupling. It is analytically impossible for DMC to decrease while DMC/GDP increases under the condition of positive GDP growth. These scenarios are illustrated in Figure 1, Panel A . Let t denote the rate of decline in resource consumption per unit of GDP (t > 0 when consumption per unit of GDP decreases, and t < 0 otherwise). Additionally, let t k represent the required rate of decrease in resource consumption per unit of GDP to maintain constant total resource consumption. The relationship between GDP growth (g) and t k is derived from Wang et al., (2013) and (Lu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013) : tk = g/(1+g) Depending on the value of t, the possibilities are depicted in Figure 1 Panel B. Economies typically experience growth, and it has generally been assumed that g > 0. However, during the study period from 2000 to 2019, some regions experienced economic contraction, where g < 0. Despite this, the definitions of absolute decoupling, decoupling, and non -decoupling remain consistent, regardless of whether economic growth g is positive or negative. In Figure 3 , zones marked "A" correspond to cases where t is positive and exceeds g/(1+g), indicating absolute decoupling. ### Data

To analyse decoupling, data were gathered on population, economic growth, and material consumption for China, Europe, the United States, and the rest of the world during 2000-2019. GDP and population data were obtained from the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD, 2024), with GDP measured at constant 2015 prices in US Dollars. For consistency, Europe (EU-28) refers to the 28 countries of the European Union, including the United Kingdom, prior to its withdrawal in 2020. Data on domestic material consumption (DMC) were sourced from the Global Material Flows Database developed by CSIRO and the International Resources Panel of the United Nations Environmental Program (CSIRO, 2024; Schandl et al., 2024) .
